utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-09-92-T, The Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. The late start is due to technical problems which have not yet been fully resolved. If there are no preliminaries, could, then, the witness be brought into the courtroom. Ms. D'Ascoli, I think you have used approximately 15 minutes, and you need 30 minute, if I --

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I think -- I checked the estimations done by the Registrar, and I think it was 11 minutes that I had used. But, yes, approximately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Mandilovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to remind that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you have given last Friday, that you'll tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. D'Ascoli will now continue her examination-in-chief. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Mandilovic. I will now have some brief questions for you, after the preliminary that we had last Friday. First of all, in your paragraph -- in your statement at paragraphs 42 to 58, you say that the state hospital was shelled in several locations, that intensity of the shelling varied in different time-periods and the hospital was hit mostly from the southern side. What I wanted to ask is whether at any point in time from May 1992 onwards, there was a flag of any kind on the hospital to indicate that the building was a medical facility?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the southern side of the state hospital building, there was a large flag of the Red Cross, stretching between the sixth and the twelfth floor. It was absolutely visible from any distance. That flag was there for some five to six months. Pardon. Later on, because of the shots fired at the hospital, burned and it was also partially destroyed by the wind and rain. Once that flag was taken off, there were no indications of that nature anymore.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. Mandilovic. I wish now to focus on the medical records from the state hospital and other Sarajevo health institutions that have you analysed and authenticated in your statement and in preparation for your testimony today. So, first of all, yes, there are a number of medical records issued by the Sarajevo state hospital itself. Do you remember reviewing and authenticating those in preparation of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I have confirmed that.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And in your statement, I think this is paragraph 116, you -- you say that you also had occasion to see medical records from the clinical centre of the University of Sarajevo and the forensic institute of the Faculty of Medicine, institutions which you say are commonly known or referred to as the Kosevo hospital; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Can you explain us the circumstances in which you had the chance to see these medical records from the clinical centre at the Kosevo hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had such opportunity every day, because the patients, be it those who were sick or wounded, kept going back and forth between the different Sarajevo medical institutions, depending on which institution was being shelled at the time. It meant the following in practical terms: If one was treated in the sate hospital, in my hospital. It doesn't necessarily mean that they had the opportunity to complete that the treatment in our institution because of the events. That is why the patients went from one institution to another all the time, and we had no -- we had occasion to follow the treatment they received at our hospital as well as at their hospital. We treated both our patients and their patients and the same thing was the other way around.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Do you think you could give us an estimate of how many -- how many medical records from the clinical centre you saw and worked with during the war between 1992 and 1995? Just an approximation. I mean, dozens, hundreds, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can speak of hundreds, for sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Okay. Let's take one example of such documents. This is one of the documents you reviewed as part of the -- the documents discussed in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Can I please have on the screens, the 65 ter number 0 -- 110222. Sorry, I just meant 10222; apologies. Mr. Mandilovic, can you see the documents on the screens?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Okay. What can you tell us about this document, and, in particular, its provenance?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document, or this specialist report, originates from the clinical centre of the Sarajevo university medical facility. We can see that in the heading in the upper right -- left-hand side corner. On the right side, we have the protocol number. In the middle, we have the facts, or, rather, the physician's conclusion that the wounding was caused by a piece of shrapnel. Underneath, we have the diagnosis in Latin, and we see what the treatment was that the patient received, and it concludes by saying that there should be an additional checkup in three days' time, followed by a signature. Based on what I can see, I assert that this is a valid medical document.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes. My question was whether, on account of your experience and of your co-operation with the clinical centre these documents and documents of this type appear to you as medical records produced during the ordinary course of the medical business of the clinical centre of the University of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. I agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Now, in performing your duties as a doctor in those years - again, 1992 to 1995 - you also co-operated with the forensic institute of the Faculty of Medicine in Sarajevo. And in your segment you say you're also familiar and was able to authenticate autopsy reports from the forensic institute. I wanted to have also an example of such documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: I would call up on the screens 65 ter 10401. If we can just have a look at the first page of the document. Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Dr. Mandilovic, I would ask you the same question, meaning what can you tell us about this document and, in particular, its provenance and whether you're able to authenticate it or not.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assert that this is it an authentic document based on the following: In the upper left-hand side corner, we see the name of the facility. We have a broader and more narrow designation. It is actually the Faculty of Medicine in Sarajevo specifically its forensics institute or its Department of Forensics. Underneath, we have some general information. There is a diagnosis in Latin, and in the lower left-hand side corner, there's a signature of an assistant at the medical faculty and a specialist of forensic medicine. In the middle, there's a stamp of the school of medicine and its forensics institute.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And, again, could you give us an approximation of how many such documents you encountered during your -- during your duties as doctor in -- in the years during the war?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Out of the entire medical documentation I was able to see, I didn't come across such documents as this too often for a simple reason. We worked with people who were still alive, who were either sick or wounded. This type of document did not arrive routinely but occasionally. In order to complete a medical file, we needed documents such as this one, in cases of patients who passed away, and it made an integral part of the file.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And, again, we can say -- can we say that you're familiar such documents and that for the way these appears, these and other similar documents appear from the forensic institute, can you say that these such documents were produced during the regular medical business of the forensic institute?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Now, there's a third document coming from a third medical institution in Sarajevo which is the Dobrinja General Hospital. Also, these type of documents are among the documents that you authenticated in your statement and also in preparation for your testimony through reviewing additional documents that we presented to you. First of all, can you tell us something more about the Dobrinja General Hospital. And maybe, in the meantime, I can call up on the screens 65 ter number 10026, please.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The General Hospital in Dobrinja is a medical facility that was set up due to the war circumstances and the fact that the city was besieged. At its location, there had been an outpatient clinic. Dobrinja, is a part of Sarajevo. It is a settlement of some 30.000 inhabitants. It is some 10 kilometres away from the centre of town. Due to the difficult circumstances surrounding the transport of the wounded and sick to the clinical centre, i.e., the state hospital, it was decided to set up a makeshift General Hospital in Dobrinja. That is how it was created. In the course of the first few months and years, I dare say, it was being equipped and provided with personnel. Its role was to take care of people and provide medical assistance to the wounded and sick in that part of Sarajevo as quickly as possible. Oftentimes I came across documents, medical documents, from the Dobrinja hospital for the reasons I have explained earlier. The wounded and sick who were in Sarajevo could not always receive treatment in the same place. That was one reason. There was another reason, which was a rule which stated that all those who were seriously wounded or sick were to be taken to the large medical facilities in town, to the centre and the state hospital, to receive assistance because they required a far greater degree of medical care.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Dr. Mandilovic -- yes, exactly. I was going to ask you about the document that now appears on the screen. And if you can tell us which are the elements that make you say that these records, these medical records come from the Dobrinja General Hospital and is an authentic document from that institution?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a typical document from the general hospital in Dobrinja. It is a discharge sheet, meaning that the patient had been hospitalised and released. He was -- or she was provided with these documents as part of their file. We have the following elements. At the top, we have the name of the medical facility which is the general hospital in Dobrinja in this case. Just underneath, in block letters, we see what kind of medical document this is. In this case, it is a discharge sheet. It is followed by some general information, including the dates of arrival and departure from hospital. Further down, we have a diagnosis in Latin, concerning the type of injury. Even further down, we have a clear description of what was done, followed by a signature in block letters and in handwriting of the physician who treated the patient. The document concludes with two round stamps of the Dobrinja General Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Mandilovic. I have one last point to address with regard to medical records and then I will conclude my examination, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Can I please have on the screens 65 ter 28623.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Dr. Mandilovic, in preparation for your testimony today were you asked to review the medical -- additional medical records to those already included in your statement and to make any observation you might have on both the authenticity of the documents and also their content. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. I looked at the medical documents which I had no occasion to see previously. Following a close inspection, it is my conclusion that the documents are original.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: If you see the chart on the screen, Dr. Mandilovic, were your observation recorded in this chart that we now see on the screens?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And did you put your initials to indicate that you believed the document to be authenticate?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: For example on the --

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: For example, on the very first page if you look at column 5 do you recognise those initials?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And if we can go to the last page of the document, of the chart, which is page 5. The English, please. The last -- the last page of the English document, please.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Do you recognise --

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certified that with my own signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sir, in reviewing the documents listed in the chart, did they appear to you as medical records produced in the course of the ordinary medical business of the Dobrinja General Hospital and the clinical centre of the University of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I had a look at that, and my conclusion was that these were original documents. It was not only from these two hospitals. I think there were also documents from the state hospital of Sarajevo. That is to say, all three medical institutions that you presented to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And are you now -- will you -- are you willing to answer any additional questions that the Defence or the Chamber might have about this chart and about the documents that you reviewed?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this point I will just -- according to our proposal I will just proceed as follows, meaning that I will postpone my tendering of both the chart with 65 ter 28623, and also of the associated exhibits that are listed in the associated exhibit part of the exhibit list for Dr. Mandilovic until after the cross-examination so that the Defence has an opportunity to put questions about these documents and their authenticity to the witness and I do so in light of the objections that the Defence raised in the -- in the response to the 92 ter motion?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: I am -- I have one just one observation. In the document chart we won't tender 65 ter 10049 because we notice it's duplicative of another 65 ter already contained in the chart meaning 65 ter 13726 which is a more complete record. So I just wanted to put that on the record. There is also -- well, also another point. There is one associated exhibit that defers from the others meaning that it is not a medical record authenticated by the witness but is an excerpt from a video showing the state hospital and also some interior scenes from the hospital. This excerpt is discussed by the witnesses at paragraphs 93 to 97 of the statement and I can tender this document at this stage because I don't think the Defence raised any objection as to that. This is the 65 ter number 22473A, a subset that we created from 65 ter 22473. It only includes a specific footage of the original video running from 01:54:03 to 01:54:56. And the video does not have any audio that we intend to rely on, therefore, I would just tender it as a public exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The 65 ter 10049 appears as number 2 in the chart, Ms. D'Ascoli, just to have that on the record. Are there any objections against the admission of the associated video?

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: The 65 ter number that I have for the video is 22473A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And I do understand that there are no objections against admission. Mr. Registrar, 22473A receives number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P682, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P682 is admitted into evidence. And we'll wait with the chart and the nine remaining documents appearing on it until after the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Dr. Mandilovic, thank you very much. I don't have further questions at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: That concludes my examination for the time being, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. D'Ascoli. Mr. Stojanovic, are you ready to cross-examine the witness? Mr. Mandilovic, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Stojanovic. Mr. Stojanovic is counsel for Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, doctor.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll be very brief. I'll go through a few areas that I wish to ask you about and that are related to your statement. As I look at your CV, it is my understanding that you were born in Novi Sad; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: That is in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serbia, the autonomous province of Vojvodina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: As a very young boy you came to Sarajevo with your family?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You finished elementary school, high school, and you got a degree in medicine in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not hear the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that in 1992 you had Yugoslav and Serbian citizenship?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yugoslav.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: We'll have to do this a bit slower. We're both very fast speakers.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that when you were born you had Serbian and Yugoslav citizenship?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At any point in time, until 1992, did you have citizenship of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Only Yugoslav citizenship.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: After doing your military service in Montenegro, you started working as a military doctor, an army doctor; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. After I completed my medical training and residency, I started working as an army doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you attend reserve officers' school for the medical corps in the army when you did your military service?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I completed that subsequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And what was the rank that you were granted then?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When did you become a professional military officer in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In 1978, you had the rank of lieutenant, and until 1992, your career advanced, and you received the rank of major; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When the war broke out, you were a member of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'd like us to look at paragraph 2 -- 23, together with you. P679 is the number it has been assigned in e-court. Please help us a bit. Tell us more specifically what this was all about. You will see paragraph 23 in front of you now. In your statement, you say that, to the best of your recollection, on the 2nd of May, there was an incident when a small group of soldiers started out from the military hospital where they were stationed and moved in the direction of the headquarters of the 2nd Military District to help out a situation with a truck. There was an incident that took place in Vojvode Stepe Street which is the right bank of the Miljacka river. "Some people were injured, and I think some were killed as well but I cannot give any figures today with any certainty." Can you tell us more specifically what was it that actually happened then, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you read out just now is something that I did not take part in. I just recounted something that had happened and that I saw in the media because, at that point in time, on the 2nd of May, I had left the hospital, and I don't know when it was that this column of JNA officers and soldiers had set out. But I found out what the exact route was and how this happened later on during the course of the day through the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What was this that you were informed about?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That an incident, an armed incident, had occurred in the street of Vojvode Stepe. A group of soldiers of the JNA and a clash with the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, these soldiers had set out to help get a truck out; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I learned from the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were these people stopped and killed?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether they were stopped or not. I just know that there was an armed conflict that there were casualties. People were wounded and killed. But how all of this actually happened, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how many dead soldiers there were?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, approximately 80 per cent of the questions you've asked the witness now find their answers in his statement. Now you are exploring something the witness acknowledges that he has no personal knowledge. He learned some of it through the media. So I wonder whether this is the right witness to ask these questions. Would you please keep that in mind when you continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I just wanted to see whether he had any other knowledge, apart from what has already been referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were any of these soldiers or officers brought to the then-military hospital to be provided with medical aid?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say because I wasn't at the hospital any longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's look at paragraph 26 of your statement. It's the same document that we have before us. This is what you say there: "When the JNA withdrew from the state hospital, it was an organised departure and equipment and drugs were left behind. The hospital had been surrounded by patriotic forces (police and Territorial Defence) and agreement had been reached that equipment would be left behind." To the best of your knowledge, when was the hospital surrounded by these patriotic forces, as you call them?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is very hard to say with any degree of accuracy. I said that in my statement too. One has to be very precise and very fair. This was not a classical military encirclement. These were groups of persons without weapons, say, from the second half of the month of April. They did not stop anyone from entering the hospital or leaving the hospital. They did not constitute any kind of specific hindrance to the flow of patients and civilians and staff who were coming and going.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were they policemen?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. No. They did -- were not wearing official police uniforms, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What was your understanding of their task? If I understand you correctly, what do you mean when you say "surrounded"?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well not surrounded. It's hard to say. It's hard to find the right word. Quite simply they were there around the hospital and in a way they were patrolling. I think that today, given this significant time distance, I believe that the motto of their stay there was to make sure that medical equipment would not leave the hospital. I think that was their only task. But, look, this is just my opinion. This is not anything official.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In this paragraph, 26, you mention that among them there were policemen. So that's why I'm asking you, whether this reminds --

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe. Oh, I really should slow down and this should be interpreted. Maybe there were a few policemen there, but it is really hard to say. You had the Territorial Defence there. And they included members of the police and members of the reserve police. Members of the reserve police are people who had no uniforms or just bits and pieces of uniforms, so it is very hard to say today whether they were policemen. So it is very hard to say. And it would be irresponsible to say anything. Whatever I would say would be unfair.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us put ourselves in the following situation. If the JNA had decided to leave its equipment -- to take its equipment out of the hospital, would that be a legitimate act?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not a legal expert, but I think the answer would be no. You know that from the 1st of March onwards, Bosnia-Herzegovina was a separate state so the JNA was a group, an armed military grouping, that did not have any elements of legality at that moment. So I think the answer would be no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You were still a member of this army that you called an illegitimate military force there, and you were a member until May?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And if you look at the recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina, was the question of property resolved? That is to say, the property of the JNA. Was that question resolved?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic now we are discussing this at state level. It is being discussed to this day. I cannot resolve it and I don't have an answer to that question either.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that. That is what I expected you to say, because in your previous answer you said that you believe that this was not JNA property. Is that correct --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, first, would you please slow down. The witness started his first answer that he wasn't a lawyer, he wouldn't know about these kind of things and he gave his personal impression. Now your last question was that you were happy with this answer, and again asked him whether it was correct what he said. What he said is on the transcript. Please move on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, if I may, I would just like to conclude the previous answer provided to Mr. Stojanovic. The JNA included members of all of the former republics of Yugoslavia. The republics financed its existence. It is not as if the JNA financed its own operations. It was financed by the Yugoslav republics. Therefore, it is very difficult to say whose equipment it was that was procured for the JNA. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By your leave, we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You said, and that is why I asked you, that it was your impression that it was the task of the TO which surrounded the hospital was to halt any taking away of the equipment. I'm asking you what is it that you base your conclusion on?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I base it on what I have said a moment ago. The work of the hospital was not hindered at any point in time. People went in and out, including patients and staff, without any problems. Therefore, I don't see any other reason than the one I mentioned. Perhaps there is something else, but I don't see it. At that point in time, I didn't think otherwise, and it is still my opinion. Of course, I have to repeat that is purely my impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did they have the means or resources to prevent any potential taking away of the equipment from the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say that I did not see armed groups of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At one point, the then-director of the hospital, Colonel Tausan, summoned to you his office. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He summoned who?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You specifically.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have a conversation with him at any point in time concerning an evacuation plan of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Not me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was it your decision to leave the hospital and your position?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you inform any of your superior officers of your decision?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Who and why; if you please.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I informed them because, one, I had to act professionally under the circumstances. I informed my first and second superior officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Who were the officers you informed?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first superior officer was Professor Lucic, my boss. The second one is Colonel Tausan, the director.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did any of the two tell you that you had to follow the orders and to leave the hospital and Sarajevo, together with the army whose member you were?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. I have to say that all managing personnel of the JNA in the hospital were quite liberal on that score.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you believe it was -- it amounted to deserting the unit and army whose member you were and on whose payroll you were acting as an officer?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Why do you believe it was not deserting the unit?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the JNA was not a legal armed formation in Bosnia-Herzegovina at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stojanovic, the Chamber unanimously fails to see the relevance of 90 per cent of your questions. Could you please reconsider during the break the questions to follow and then put relevant questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will conclude with this. However, by your leave, I'd like to put just one more question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One more question before we take a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: We'll look at paragraph 31 of your statement together. It is Exhibit P679. Doctor, in your conversation with the Prosecution, you said something different, and that is why I thought it might prove to be relevant. In paragraph 31 you say: "It was difficult to make this decision because remaining behind when one's unit leaves is, in effect, desertion. As a professional soldier, it is a step not to be undertaken lightly." However, what you say today is contrary to it. You say today that you believe that your decision had not meant deserting the unit. I'm asking you simply whether what you said in the statement, which is now part of the exhibits in this case which you provided some time ago, is an incorrect interpretation, or did you change your position in the meantime?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Legally speaking, I am of the same view. However, speaking as a human being and a colleague, it was a difficult decision to make. Legally it was not wrong to make it. Speaking as a human being, of course, it was difficult because I had worked with those people for a number of years. However, in the context of everything I've said thus far, legally speaking, it was not a wrong decision to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will take a break, and we'll resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, you may proceed. Could I remind both you and you, Mr. Mandilovic, to make a short pause between question and answer and answer and question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We'll do our best. Could we please have 553, page 24 in e-court. It is a photograph from the Sarajevo court finder album, which we've had occasion to see it previously. I wanted to ask the witness to assist us in identifying certain features and buildings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that you referred to P3, page 24 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P3. Precisely, Your Honour. Line 15, page 22, that's what it should read: P3. Page 24. Thank you. Could we please zoom in on this photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Doctor, do you recognise what's in the picture and tell us if you can see the military hospital building there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can find my bearings here, and I can see the military hospital building.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask the usher to provide a pen for the witness, in order to be able to mark the military hospital building.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, doctor. Since we'll be making some further markings, let's stay with this photograph. Am I right in saying that this photograph was taken from the southern side of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When you mentioned that the building was damaged most intensely on this side, that would be the side that we can see en face now; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Doctor, how far were the lines of the two warring parties in this part of Sarajevo, especially viewing it from the hospital building?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is difficult to be precise. I've tried to explain it before. I think it was some 400 metres, as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Between what?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between the military hospital and the lines of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So between the two line, the hospital and the positions held by Republika Srpska army. But between those two lines, there were positions of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If there was an exchange of fire from those positions, am I right in saying that the fire from the positions of the Army of Republika Srpska was directed in -- towards the southern side of the hospital building?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct. The military hospital was not a defence line. I can defend -- presume where the defence lines were, although I never visited those lines, but they were far closer to the Serb positions than the military position was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: My question was this: If the VRS were to fire shots at the positions of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, would that be in the same direction as the southern side of the hospital building?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in terms of direction. But physically speaking, it is impossible because there's a difference in altitude, if you want to go into detail. The Army of Republika Srpska always assumed vantage points over the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the -- their shots went downwards, not towards the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that in this photograph such buildings that are not at an elevation but close to the Miljacka river, that such buildings were the same level, the same altitude, as the positions of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe the question is not clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me try it this way. Am I right that the buildings you see here which is Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And Grbavica was in the hands of the VRS, those buildings were level with the positions of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the other bank of the Miljacka river?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. Part of Grbavica was in the hands of the VRS but on Trebevic and the Jewish cemetery it was also the VRS who were there and such positions were at a significantly higher altitude.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: We'll discuss that further. For the time being, I'd like to ask you this: Do you know and did you at any point in time learn that the positions of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina were in the buildings marked in this photograph as buildings number 4 and 5 in -- near Trebevic and the Unis building?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I don't know what the tactical situation was of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I really don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's look at a document together, which is in e-court. It is 1D546?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, let me ask you this for the time being, technically speaking we need to save this photograph or we will loose the markings. Perhaps the witness could mark it only with a VB, "vojna bolnica," military hospital or state hospital, and could we please assign it a number because I am about to move to another document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Doctor, would you be so kind as to use the pen and please the letters DB, "drzavna bolnica," state hospital, and I would kindly ask the Court to assign a number to this marked photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, marked version of Exhibit P3 shall be assigned Exhibit D127. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D127 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 1D546 next.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the document, doctor, let me ask you this: Did you know that the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina had sniper positions close to the hospital where you worked? Were you ever told that at any point in time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I had no such knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any information pertaining to the sniping units which were part of the 1st Corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The operation of sniper units in any army is a military secret. I was in no position to deal with such issues. I was a medical expert and I was treated as such. All such matters pertaining to the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina is something that I can improvise my answers on, but I have no specific information.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I understand that. That is why I'm asking you whether you were certain that the hospital building was hit by sniper fire or infantry fire at any point in time.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, in the 44 months of the siege, the state hospital was hit from all sorts of weapons. Let me be specific: Infantry weapons, all the way up to shells and projectiles.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: However, given what you have said a moment ago, you cannot confirm whether in the total of infantry fire that hit the hospital there were any sniping shots that hit it.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't make that difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us look at the document next. It is an Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina document dated the 2nd of October, 1993. It reads: "On the basis of the necessity for more quality training and more quality performance of duties by snipers, in the 1st, 2nd, and 3rd Motorised Battalion," I presume mtb, and the original stands for motorised battalion, "for all those reasons a sniper squad" -- actually, "a sniper platoon is being established," and we have the names of the people involved. I presume, first and foremost, that you have never had occasion to see this document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: However, appreciating the fact that you spent a number of years in Sarajevo, can you tell us how far from the state hospital was the Blagoje Parovic school?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, I take it there's no need to remind you that the first line of paragraph 47 says: "Whilst I cannot say that the hospital was deliberately sniped at, I must say that the hospital received thousands of hits from small-arms fire, and photographs taken at the time of the war show the hospital to be bullet-riddled, and greatly damaged." Which clearly indicates that this witness apparently has not formed an opinion on sniping, apart from what he saw. That is, the east, the west and the south part of the building, being hit by small-arms fire. So, therefore, to explore in detail snipers where this witness does not even claim that from either side, I wonder to what extent that would assist the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by your leave, I would like to draw your attention to paragraph 49 of the same statement. The witness's previous testimony is being quoted there, and it says clearly that between August 1994 and November 1995 the main hospital building was exposed both to artillery fire and to sniper fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you look at the building, you wouldn't be surprised by that, isn't it? If you see photographs and if you see a video. I mean, he doesn't form any opinion about who sniped, who shelled. At least that's not in these paragraphs. That's -- should be clear as a starting point from putting any further questions to what the witness states. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I conclude on that note. Because the witness cannot say on this basis whether the weapons included snipers, and in paragraph 47, there was a reference to deliberate targeting of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And, doctor, now I'd like to go back to the question that I had put to you. Can you tell us, at all, how far away the Blagoje Parovic school was from the state hospital, that is?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether we mean the same school. There where many schools in the city of Sarajevo. I think it is a few kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me, to the best of your knowledge, do you know where the Cenex building was?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. It is certainly 4 to 5 kilometres away from the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then I'm not going to be using this document any longer, Your Honours. We will tender it through another witness then, so I have no intention of using it any further now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Doctor, I'd like to ask you the following: Could you tell us how far away the closest police station was from the hospital, in this area, in Marin Dvor, in that part of town?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Marin Dvor police station is relatively close to the hospital. It is perhaps 200 metres away. 200, 250 maybe?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was the mentioned police station operational during the war as well?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, look, I was not at the police station. But it was certainly used for this function for the comings and goings of policemen. I can provide a non-medical opinion now. It could not have had any combat function because it is within the group of buildings there. It is a very densely populated area, Marin Dvor. It's a proper city area, so this is not a facility that would be any kind of threat to the other side. If I can be even more specific. This was - and still is - only an administrative building and nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Now I have to ask you about this, doctor. Are you trying to say that a police station in war time and the police as part of the armed forces is not a military target?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in a narrower sense, it is a military target.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, doctor.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But it is a target that is not active. I don't know whether you understand what I'm trying to say. On the roof of the Marin Dvor police station, there wasn't a sniper nest or a machine-gun nest or something like that. This was a purely administrative building that was used for such purposes only.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: How come you know that, doctor if you said a few moments ago --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's -- let's limit ourselves to -- Mr. Stojanovic, there's no need to make this kind of gesture nodding no. Let's -- the doctor indicated that he gave his non-medical opinion. The Chamber appreciates that he wants to assist, but let's stick to the factual knowledge of the witness. Apart from military target or not, Mr. Mandilovic, you said the building was used for administrative purposes. Could you explain - because that's what Mr. Stojanovic would like to know - what is the source of your knowledge that it was exclusively used for administrative purposes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, because before the war and during the war and after the war, its purpose remained the same. This is the administrative centre of the police that takes care of the Marin Dvor zone and a bit beyond that. It's a small building that is irrelevant. People came and went and perhaps there was a place there where they assembled but, I mean, it cannot constitute by its very configuration a place from where one could fire or engage in combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Doctor, at the time, during the war, was the state building -- hospital building secured?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only at the gate of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Who provided security there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the gate, there were reserve policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Administratively, did they belong to the police station that you talked about a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is easily possible. I don't know where the command or -- the police was, the reserve police, and -- I don't know how this division functioned. But the important thing is that at the hospital gate, there were only reserve policemen during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, doctor, is it correct that, at that time, there was a medical battalion within the 1st Corps of the BH army in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And where were its headquarters?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The medical battalion within the 1st Corps was stationed -- well, practically it was deployed in the field around Sarajevo. It was within the Territorial Defence units. So it is hard to say where it was stationed. You are probably referring to the question of medical facilities near the hospital. This was just a clinic, but it wasn't the headquarters of the medical battalion. The medical battalion was stationed within the administration of the 1st Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Within the state hospital, was there a headquarters of that battalion there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The state hospital was a non-military formation throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Where was the command of the medical battalion?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I really don't know where it was. I assume that the chief of the medical unit of the 1st Corps was in the command of the 1st Corps, which would be perfectly logical.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we please look at 1D547, the statement of the witness, Mr. Mandilovic, dated the 5th of January, 2007. And could we please take a look at paragraph 18. 1D547 is the number of the document. I'm repeating it once again. Could we please focus on paragraph 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mandilovic --

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't got anything in front of me yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise your signature -- well, actually, I'll ask you about that later. Please look at paragraph 18 of the statement that you gave to the investigators of the Tribunal on the 5th of January, 2007. And this is what you say there. I'm reading the third sentence from paragraph 18: "The medical corps battalion was housed in the hospital ... complex. This comprised of the medical support unit of the 1st Corps of the ABiH." This is what I'm asking you now: What kind of unit was this?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, you read the first statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The third and fourth one.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I read out the end?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: "The medical corps battalion was housed in the hospital complex. This comprised of the medical support unit of the 1st Corps of the ABiH. Although this was called a battalion, it" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "... only comprised of medical personnel such as doctors, nurses, et cetera. The medical corps battalion was exclusively used to treat soldiers who were recovering from injury and illness."

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: This is what I'm asking you now: What kind of battalion are you speaking of here, that was housed within the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am referring to two things here. The 1st Corps has to have its own medical support and that is the medical battalion that consisted of doctors, medical technicians and equipment, and it is supposed to take care of persons who were wounded and ill. That is quite clear. However, the medical battalion is not a stationary institution. It is an institution that is out in the field. It is in units of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina specifically. Less there be any confusion here, this is what I'm saying here: That it only consisted of medical personnel for one clinic or infirmary, so it was this one infirmary that was used for recovery of patients who had been injured so the question of the medical battalion is one thing. And the second question would be what was near the hospital in this respect? So I am categorically stating and it can be seen from this context too that near the hospital there was only this infirmary with doctors and nurses who were working there, and who took care of patients, wounded persons, sick persons who required longer treatment but not hospitalisation. So it was only a small medical institution?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Doctor, where was that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That facility is to the west of the hospital. To the west of the buildings of the military hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us for the transcript how far away it is from the hospital building.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps 250 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, doctor. Could we please take a look at P3 again. P3, the photograph that we saw a moment ago. Page 24. And while we're waiting, doctor, let me just ask you the following. The police station, Marin Dvor, can it be seen in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only the roof, maybe. Well, I'll try. I'll try to be fully co-operative. But from the position that is provided here, this picture from the south, it is hard to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The upper right-hand part of the photograph, could that be zoomed in, please. This is what I'm ask you now, now that we have this zoomed in. Can we mark the roof of the police station?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's here.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not hear Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would this be right? Oh, I see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we again zoom in to the part we saw a minute ago.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Doctor, could you please mark this with a PS, police station.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Doctor, the north part of the hospital building was safer during the war, and it was used for treating patients who had been wounded, and also medical staff were housed there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that the intensity of fire from the north was considerably less than from the other side?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The front line between the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Army of Republika Srpska, if we look at the north, from the northern part of the building, how far away was it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is hard to say because I did not tour the area, you know, but roughly, it is known where the positions of the Army of Republika Srpska were up there, Mrkovici, Poljane. I'm talking about that segment up there. So, at any rate, the distance is far greater as the crow flies than is the one on the southern side.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you give us an estimate of how far away this was in kilometres?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's very difficult. Even an artillery officer could not tell you for sure. Well, okay. Let me venture a guess. Three kilometres, as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Doctor, could you tell the Court whether, as one looks towards the north to the positions of the VRS, were there any elevations or buildings that were taller than the hospital building?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the north? Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There were no taller buildings in that direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Is Kosevsko Brdo in that direction?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Partially. Partially. The other part was completely clear and free.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Is Kosevo hill at a higher elevation and the hospital building?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a bit. But it's not a building. You asked me about buildings, whether there were any buildings or facilities taller than the military hospital. And this is a hill.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... there may be a problem here. I understood the question to relate to both buildings and higher positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps I can clear this up, Your Honour. I think we're moving in the right direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What I want to ask you is this, doctor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the language which we find on the transcript is elevations. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So, let me repeat, doctor, and you can see why I'm asking this, because of infantry fire. Between the positions held by the VRS for which you knew were at Mrkovici and Poljane --

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In part. I can't be precise. I never toured those lines. But it's an approximation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And the military or state hospital building, there are elevations, hills, and buildings taller than the military hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is Kosevo hill but only partially. If you look at the picture, the photograph, if you look closely, you see that it is only the western part of the military hospital is in the direction of that elevation. The eastern part is completely clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: We agree --

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To put it in a different way. To the west of the military hospital high-rise, there is this elevation called Kosevo hill. But the other sides of the -- that area were far lower and clear of obstacles.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: On the northern side, while you were in the hospital, was any infantry fire directed at that part of the building, of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't remember -- well, perhaps there may have been some. I cannot be very specific. However, I think there was no infantry fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Doctor, the entrance to the hospital was on the northern side of the building; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The entrance was on the southern side.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: During the war --

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: During the war, did you always use only the southern entrance?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Always. It is the official entrance. That is where the staff gate is and the vehicle gate is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: During the war, you used four floors. Only the lowest four floors of the buildings as the safest ones; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Stojanovic, which building specifically?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are three buildings in the hospital compound. There is the high-rise of 12 floors. To the left of the high-rise, there is a lower building with four floors. And to the right of the high-rise, there's a three-storey building. It all makes the state hospital compound in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In the high-rise, there are 12 floors.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: My question is this: How many floors did you use in that building or in that part of the state hospital compound?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One cannot be specific in answering that for the simple reason that the fire directed at the state hospital was not always of the same intensity. It all depended on our needs. When there was heavy shelling, we left the southern part of the building and went down to the lower floors, including the cellar, the basement. When there was no combat, when there was no shelling, the patients were again returned up to the fourth floor, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Having in mind the capacity of the hospital before the war, in terms of percentages, how much of its capacity was put to use during the war?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a difficult question. It's a statistical matter. At least 80 per cent. Because, let me make things easier for you. Before the war, or in peacetime, there were other hospital standards in application. There were three-bed rooms only. There was a maximum of three beds per room. But during the war, one cannot respect such standards. There were situations where we had rooms used where the staff used to change. In peacetime we placed between 20 and 25 beds which is completely against any medical and hygiene standards, but were necessary in order to survive.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Doctor, now that we have this southern side in the picture, you mentioned that the VRS positions were at elevations at Grbavica as compared to the positions of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The toponyms, Debelo Brdo and Colina Kapa, do they ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Debelo Brdo, I have never heard of that expression, not until the war and after that. As for Colina Kapa, it is an elevation at a distant end of town from the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Who held those two elevations?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. There are two questions in this: Who held those positions; and who controlled that area. Because to hold and control is not the same thing. That's one thing. Another thing: These were tactical positions, and the ownership, so to say, changed, depending on the movements of the forces. I'd rather not speculate as to who held them and when during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well, doctor. I will not press this any further because you've -- you were asked about this in the Karadzic case. Let me move on. In your amalgamated statement, you said that in no time you had an opportunity to see the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina fire mortars from the school -- the hospital compound on or near the compound?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. I'm very proud and happy to be able to say that. I state that categorically, although I wasn't in the hospital around the clock. However during the long period I was there, I never saw any weapons in and around the hospital. That's the first thing --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me stop you there because you prompted another question. According to your statement you worked for 24 hours and then had a break of another 24 hours when you rotated in regular shifts; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Nominally speaking. However, in real terms, it was never like that because in certain periods you could observe the 24-hour shifts but there were many periods when one worked all the time, when there was no time to rest or leave. I have to say that much of the time in the 44 months I was in the hospital much more than at home. That is why I can say competently that during the time that I was on duty, I never saw any weapons in and around the hospital. I started answering that, but you interrupted me, Mr. Stojanovic. Let me continue. First of all, I need to say that the surroundings of the hospital is this: It is an urban hospital. There is no extra space. Even parking spaces are very limited. Another thing. Pardon me, Mr. Stojanovic. Another thing: The hospital was always - how should I put it? - it was always observed by UNPROFOR, the UN, the foreign media, and none of them, nobody ever noticed any fire from the hospital. That is why I wanted to put my statement in -- in a wider context. And thank you for allowing me to do so, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, doctor. I asked you this for the simple reason that we had occasion to see -- to hear UNPROFOR testimony here to that effect. Can you exclude the possibility that in your absence from the hospital it could have happened that there was a mobile vehicle used to fire mortars?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm speaking as a non-medical expert. Yes, of course. But not from the hospital. It could only be done from the street surrounding the hospital, not from the hospital. Technically speaking, it would have been impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, doctor. When you say you went home, tell us how far was your home from the state hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some 3 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And you traversed that route, if not daily, then, very frequently, on foot and onboard the hospital bus; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It all depended on the situation in the city at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Along that route, from home to the hospital, did you pass by the Alpina building, as we called it, in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you tell me what is Alpina? I remember it only as a Slovenian company selling shoes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: They had a building with a shop there produced by Alpina, the Slovenian company. We called it in popular terms, the Alpina building. Did you pass by that building?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must have. It was called the so-called Salvation Road because it was the safest route in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: How far is that building from the state hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At least 500 metres. At least.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have occasion when passing by that building along Trscanska Street to observe the command of a war-time unit of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Really, no. Walking up and down that street I could observe members of the HVO, but I had no idea where their headquarters were, and I never went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, doctor. I'll move on to a number of questions concerning the parts of the building that were hit. In your view, doctor, when you say "artillery pieces," what kind of weapons would those be that were used to hit the hospital building?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult to say. It's difficult to say. I cannot speculate as to what the calibre was. But when you see damage on the facade, when you see damage in -- in a patient room, when there's a detonation which shakes up the entire building, of course, it's a large-calibre weapon. One needn't be a military expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I understood, in the four years of the war, you had one occasion to be close to the place that was hit by heavy shelling.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was on the staircase of the hospital, and there was this enormous blast, the shaking of the ground and the shattering of glass. In the hospital corridor there was much dust. We were all grey and black, covered completely in our face and our clothes. It was a very strong detonation which luckily enough did not injure or kill anyone but occurred very closely, some 15 metres away. We were in the inside corridor. And there were no injuries or wounded people.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If you tried, could you tell us when it was?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was in the summer of 1994. I do remember it rather clearly. I believe it was in the summer of 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At any point in time, apart from this, was anyone fatally wounded by shelling in the hospital, throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so, but there were persons who were injured. There were about ten persons who were injured. That's for sure. Patients, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: That's what I'm going to ask you, doctor. But let us take this step by step. We'll do it quickly. We will agree that as for patients and hospital staff, no one was fatally wounded.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in hospital. Look, as far as I know, to the best of my knowledge, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You are testifying about what you know.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, during the four years of war, no one was killed at the state hospital as a result of shelling and small-arms fire that hit the hospital, no patients, no hospital staff.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in the hospital itself. But outside the hospital compound, there were injuries, but not in the hospital itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During these four years of war, if I understand you correctly, there about ten cases when patients were wounded by artillery that fired at the state hospital.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I have to make a small correction. It was also as a result of sniper fire. That's why I insisted on that. I insisted that we show the entire hospital. In addition to that sky-scraper that I talked about a moment ago, 12 storeys high, white, to the west there is a four-storey building. That is where our patients were also put up because our premises were overcrowded --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the end of the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Now I'm going to ask you something else. When you say "sniper wounding," are you referring to snipers or small-arms fire, or are you saying that you cannot tell what the origin of the fire was?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, it's very hard to say whether it's sniper fire or small-arms fire. But in view of the distance, and in view of the precision, it is to be assumed that it is sniper fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's refrain from assumptions at this moment. Could we first go back to your previous answer, because the interpreters did not catch all of it. You said, when you were referring to the four-storey buildings: "That is where our patients were also put up because our premises were overcrowded." What did you then add to that line.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this is what I said: That because our premises were overcrowded and because it was impossible to organise hospitalisation in the taller buildings, we had full capacity at the lower floors. So, to the west of hospital, there's this four-storey building and that was full because we had many of our patients staying there, and I think we had incidents twice that occurred there. Persons were wounded by light infantry fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, going back to the other matter of small-arms fire or sniper fire, where you say "it is to be assumed that it is sniper fire," that assumption is based of a far-away source of fire, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] An absolutely far-away source of fire. Since it was the fourth floor, the line would perhaps - perhaps - correspond to -- I mean, well, far-away fire that came from the positions of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What perhaps happened is not what we are seeking to hear from a witness.
