Do I understand that when you're talking about small-arms fire or sniper fire, that you are talking about -- talking about people that were wounded by small-calibre projectiles -- well, to -- in ordinary language, by bullets?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, patients were hospitalised because of previous wounds. They had been wounded by small-arms fire or shrapnel, but they were additionally wounded while lying in hospital. Their lower limbs were injured by fire that came from light weapons, or, rather, fire that did not have any major effect. Basically these were entry/exit wounds. Our assumption -- our assumption is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. What your assumption is is not what this Chamber would like to hear. You observed that the additional wounding was by small-arms fire, entry/exited wounds. Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic. When I said "please proceed," perhaps I should have said let's take a break. Could the witness first be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Stojanovic, you failed to tender the marked photograph where the police station was marked by the witness. Now there's no need to do that. I'll put on the record what the witness marked. On the photograph which was shown to him, which is page 24 in e-court from P3, the witness marked a roof, a building, with a red roof, which is found at the extreme right edge of this photograph, to the right of the Assembly building, which is marked by 4, where we see a church, at least a structure with a tower immediately to the right of that blue tower marked 4. And it is the building immediately to the right of that church up to where the photograph ends which was marked by the witness as the police station. It's hereby on the record. We take a break, and we'll resume at 20 minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Meanwhile, I missed that the marked photograph, which disappeared from our screen, had been saved. Could we have a look at it in e-court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because, rather than using my description, it would be good to have it marked -- to have it admitted into evidence. Well, it's disappeared now again, but ... Mr. Registrar, the number for the marked photograph.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, second marked version of Exhibit P3 shall be assigned Exhibit D128.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. You may proceed, Mr. Stojanovic. Could you give us an indication as to how much time you'd still need?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I had originally said that the examination would not take more than two hours, and I believe that we are going to do it that way. Up to two hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Doctor, I would just like us to complete that set of questions that dealt with artillery fire hitting the hospital. You personally were not in a position to see the positions from which the hospital had been hit; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. I was not in a situation to see the exact place from where the projectile had come.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, doctor. And, to conclude, in view of your education and training, you are not sure what artillery piece was used when the hospital had been hit.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I can give an approximate answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask you to say that you cannot answer, to simply say so, because you are not supposed to speculate. If you're saying that you're going to give an approximate answer --

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Stojanovic, let me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One -- one second, please. Yes. If -- if you ask the question in order to hear a no from the witness, it's the witness who answers, Mr. Stojanovic. It's not you who tell him what the answer is you would expect and you would consider appropriate. Let the witness tell us what answer he wanted to give. Please tell us your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot agree with the question that was put in the singular. The hospital was shelled all the time. It was hit all the time. So, during 44 months of the siege, it was constantly exposed to fire. It is hard for me to say exactly what the calibres were of the projectiles that had hit the hospital. However, in view of the damage that could be seen on the hospital, it was clear that it had to be large calibres because the devastation was enormous, not only of the facade itself, but also the interior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us what you consider to be "large calibres." What do you have approximately on your mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Large calibres? I think that these are cannon shells, mortar shells, a 120 millimetres. I also think it would be an anti-aircraft gun.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Doctor, could you please tell us during those four years how many such large-calibre projectiles hit the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tens. As can be seen by this large-scale devastation of the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us, to the best of your recollection, during which period of the war did this happen most often and most intensively?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the period of 1992/1993 was more intensive than what followed. Of course, there were hits in 1994 and 1995 as well, but the intensity was somewhat less.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us deal with energy supplies for the hospital. As far as electricity is concerned, do you know from which part of the grid you received electricity?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know from which part we received this form of energy, but I know that we did a lot of surgery and other work in a situation when we had to use power generators because, obviously, there had been no electricity.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that that would be the case in -- in that entire part of the city. It wasn't only the hospital that didn't have electricity.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Practically the entire city did not have electricity.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And what about these power generators? Which energy did they use?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oil.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how the oil supplies and oil derivatives reached the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was thanks to UNPROFOR. Because this was totally within their control. There was no other way. Nothing else was possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In that period, did you receive medicine and medical supplies through UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, we received medicine and medical supplies from different NGOs, humanitarian organisations, but they were always escorted by UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In order to get to the hospital and Sarajevo, they had to go through areas that were under the control of the Army of Republika Srpska; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: As for water supplies, do you know from where the hospital obtained its water and where it was that the waterworks went?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know where the source of the water supply for that area of Sarajevo was before the war?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, the city of Sarajevo has a special configuration. It is surrounded by mountains with an abundance of water. So I believe that a big city like Sarajevo was not supplied only from a single source. I assume that you are referring to Bacevo that was in Ilidza. But I believe that there were other sources as well. However, these are questions that I never dealt with seriously, and I never needed to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But you did mention Bacevo as a source of water. Will we agree that during the war, it was in the area controlled by the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bacevo was the major source of water supply, and it is true that it was controlled by the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that on the hill of Mojmilo, that was also under the control of the Army of Republika Srpska, there were reservoirs for the water supply of the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were some water facilities, but I could not tell you what the exact capacity would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In military terms, who held the area where the water tanks were at Mojmilo hill that were used to supply water for Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were probably controlled by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When you couldn't rely on the public water supply system, you used water trucks to supply the hospital; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Where did that water come from? Where did the trucks bring that water from?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where from, but I remember that the trucks were escorted by UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So the hospital either received water from the public water system or from the water trucks that were escorted by UNPROFOR during the war; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I disagree with the way you put this. We did have water, but the bare minimum. Not to the amount that would be required for the normal functioning of a hospital. We always had to save water; thus, disabling the entire hospital to function according to normal hygiene standards.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I presume you are trying to say peacetime standards, where you had to function according to war-time standards?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: As regards electricity, during the four years of war, the hospital did have electricity, either from the electrical grid or by way of its own production, because you mentioned the electricity generators.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are correct in saying that. However, one needs to remark that generators that used oil provided much more electricity in terms of percentage, in terms of the overall needs of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the hospital use gas to heat its facilities?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What kind of resources were used to heat the building facility during the four years of war?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing was used. Or, rather, we had some generator-generated electricity but that was insufficient to heat the building to any reasonable degree.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that the rest of the city had the same problems, as regards heating of housing units?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The problems we shared were very similar or maybe even more severe on their side.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Doctor, in terms of medical supplies, save for the medical humanitarian organisations you mentioned, were there any other sources of providing supplies to the state hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there were no other sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any stocks, any reserves left behind by the JNA following its departure?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were some reserves which assisted us greatly during the first year of the war, in order to assist the wounded and the sick.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When the JNA left the hospital in 1992, the JNA did not take away any of the medical equipment or stocks of medical supplies and drugs.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, they didn't take away anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to providing care to the wounded when people were injured as part of the war, you also provided regular medical services to people whose condition had nothing to do with the war.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In your report and your statement, you also deal with certain percentages. Can you tell us during the four years what was the percentage of the so-called regular medical services provided by the hospital to Sarajevo inhabitants and what was the percentage of its services lent to those who were wounded as part of the war activities?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot make that distinction. I can only mention one piece of information which may be relevant. During the 44 months of the war, there were about 9.000 operations that were carried out. The percentage you asked about may well be relevant, but there are services that were in charge of statistics. Every checkup and operation was registered, and it could be found. I don't know any figures off the cuff, because such statistics did not tell me much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Doctor, you were not in the hospital when the Markale I incident took place in February 1994; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not in the hospital. However, when I learned of the event, I arrived in the hospital in the afternoon. However, I wasn't there when the first shell struck and when the initial wounded arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You were in the hospital when the Markale II incident occurred, and you were on duty that day; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection, you explain it in your statement, where you say that you heard a single artillery shot. Do you stand by that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, correct. I stand by my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Please tell the Court, if you know, Dr. Najdanovic and do you know what his fate was, since he was a work-mate of yours?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Najdanovic was quite older than myself. He was a professor of the School of Medicine in Sarajevo. He taught surgery. His speciality was the thoracic surgeon. When I studied he was one of my lecturers. Now, as for how he died, that's something I don't know even now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Please tell the Court something about the medical documents you have inspected, as provided to you by my learned friend from the Prosecution. Those documents are now in the table we have. Let me ask you this: Did you notice in any of the documents that the -- there were some handwritten remarks on the original document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't notice any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Doctor, is it possible that while a patient is being received and hospitalised during regular checkups or upon release, after the release documentation was created, that there were some additions by the competent physician, something added to the documents once the documentation was completed?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is possible. I didn't pay much attention to that. When I went through the medical documents, I only wanted to see whether they had the elements which would confirm its authenticity and the diagnosis clearly stated in the Latin language. I didn't read everything. I didn't read through every single treatment and hospital stay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If I understand properly, by signing the documents, you confirm their authenticity, in terms of their format. Am I correct in concluding that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You could not go into whether a particular document was changed at any moment as opposed to its original version.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't check that. But at a first glance, I didn't notice any such instances.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Out of the ten documents that were shown to you, doctor, that were made part of the table relied on by the Prosecution, was there a single document which originated from your -- your hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I inspected a great deal of documents, and there were some from my hospital. I don't know whether they were from that part of the table you referred to, but they were documents from my hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I will conclude with the following question: Doctor, looking at one such document, I can tell that you a patient had been wounded, provided medical assistance and hospitalised in the Dobrinja hospital. You mentioned that as the new makeshift hospital. His treatment was concluded in Dobrinja --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, if you would guide us to the document which you are referring to so that we can follow your question and the answer. Which one is it on the chart? Which number?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Yes, Your Honour, it is a 65 ter document, 09996 of the 4th of February, 1994. It is the first document in the table. And provided you allow me to use some additional seconds, we can try to bring it up on our screens. It is 65 ter 09996.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Doctor, when we look at that document, it is the shortest document, and I used that as example only to determine the methodology that was used. It was issued by the General Hospital at Dobrinja; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: It concludes with the specialist's finding. We have a Latin diagnosis. You cannot, based on this document, tell me that at any point in time you saw or observed this patient Eldar Hafizovic. You did not have an opportunity to treat him medically. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, there is no claim whatsoever it -- the chart was introduced as giving comments on what is read -- what is -- what you can read it in. There is no claim, as far as I understand, that this witness has ever seen or treated any of these patients. So, therefore, I do not understand why, where this is obvious, it should be asked. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So -- thank you, Your Honour. I am of the same view. That is why I asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So what do you base your certification of authenticity of this document on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, if you have the same view as the Prosecution, then it is not the reason to ask the question but that's a reason not to ask the question because there is no disagreement about that, apparently. Witness, could you answer the question which was next put to you, apart from the comments you gave already regarding the authenticity. Is there anything to be added -- heading, a logo of Dobrinja hospital, date of the report, signature of the doctor, as it is said who presently works at the Sarajevo State Hospital and a stamp of the Dobrinja General Hospital, is there anything in addition to that which supported your conclusion that this appears to be an authentic document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is an authentic document. I agree. I have no other remarks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: By your leave, please look at the version in B/C/S, in the upper right-hand side corner. Is there something in handwriting; and, if so, can you read it.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Please read it out.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The massacre at Dobrinja."

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Is that in the English version?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Doctor, as part of medical documentation, should there be something like this, stating "the massacre at Dobrinja"?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards medical documentations -- documentation and those terms, the document is immaculate. As for the handwritten remark, perhaps the files were statistically treated and classified as such, and that is why we see the -- the note. That's what I can't say. But, medically speaking, the document is perfect.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who may have written that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that this should not have become a part of a medical document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, narrowly speaking. But I'm simply trying to explain why that could have been written. Probably to show or to indicate where this person was wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: However, you, on the basis of this document, which you verified medically speaking, cannot say anything about where he had been wounded; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, doctor. I have no further questions of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I would like to thank the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stojanovic. Ms. D'Ascoli, I think it would be appropriate to have a full translation of this document, including the handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, we will provide this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is there any need to re-examination the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Just a couple of questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Dr. Mandilovic, you were asked by my colleague from the Defence about the Marin Dvor police station, and you said that, as far as you know, this police station was used only as an administrative building during the war. Do you remember that part of your testimony today; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Now, my question is whether you ever saw or heard of armed fires or sniper fire coming from the building or from the roof of the police stations.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: You also said that you were asked about that, that there were reserve policemen providing security at the gate of the state hospital. Now, can you tell us which type of security this was, the one that there was a -- policemen were providing, and whether people were able to go in and out of the hospital freely?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In war time, and, after all in peacetime as well, but particularly in war time you have to have an official organ that conducts checks at the entrance into a hospital. I also have to say the following: All of those who found it necessary to go to hospital could enter and leave without any problem whatsoever. As far as the reserve of police is concerned, I have to say something else. Armed soldiers could not visit the hospital. They all had to leave their weapons at a particular place. So during the war it was thanks to these reserve policemen that the hospital was totally, totally safe from that point of view. The word itself, reserve police, tells you a lot about the level or category of such a unit. It is the lowest possible security level, if you will. What I'm trying to say is that even through this security aspect, you see what the function was and what its interest was, from a security point of view.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Okay. And then my last question is about the presence of the medical battalion in the hospital complex. While you were at the hospital -- so given you said in your previous answers today that, yes, this medical battalion was at the hospital and you clarified in which functions. Now, while you were at the hospital, was there any fire, infantry or sniping, coming from the buildings of the state hospital or from the compound of the hospital from what you could see or hear of?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, from the hospital or into the hospital? What is your question exactly?

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: From the hospital buildings, from the compound of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never. Never saw that. I've already said that quite a few times. And I've already said that it's not only my opinion but it's also the opinion of other organisations that were involved in safety and security in the field, like UNPROFOR and others.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: That concludes my re-examination, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. D'Ascoli.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has no questions. Have -- has the re-examination triggered any need for further questions, Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we still have to deal with the chart and underlying documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: So I would tender at this point both the chart which is 65 ter 28623. And the underlying documents with the exception of the document -- listed in number 2; that is, 65 ter 10049.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we shall oppose the position taken by the Prosecution to have this kind of table admitted. Because from out point of view it basically means production of documents. In each rubric number 1, it says which incident that is about, and then that is not contained in the document referred to. Then there's also --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. One second. Is the Prosecution going to rely on the handwritten text --

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- in the first document?

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: No, no, absolutely, Your Honours. And just one comment with regard to the description. The description of the exhibits, it is -- well, this is schedule victims either killed or wounded during the specific shelling and sniping incident. And you can find those names, of course, on the Prosecution's schedules. The reference is just for ease of reference of the party, and clearly it is -- it is not -- you know, it doesn't describe the -- doesn't refer to the content of the document but it is to make a cross reference between the -- the name of the person to whom the document refers to, and the schedule sniping and shelling incidents in the Prosecution schedules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, I do understand that the Prosecution says, All these persons are related to incidents which were in the -- are Scheduled Incidents and, therefore, on the basis of other documentation, I take it the -- the fact that the person mentioned in this medical documentation was involved in such an incident will be proven elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. On the basis of other documentation, on the basis of witness testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: But, you know [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, therefore, we have here documentation, as the Prosecution claims, related to victims of Scheduled Incidents, just the medical part of it, the Prosecution not relying on this handwritten text. Could you further elaborate on your objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I'm not going to object, if they will not rely on the handwritten parts and also on other descriptions. Because we really do not object to the medical documentation itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now we have seen only one handwritten portion. Are there any other handwritten portions which cause problems? Mr. Stojanovic, have you identified any other as any other handwriting similar to one on document number 1 which you considered to be inappropriate?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At this point in time, I don't have any originals here except for the table. But I think I have found something else. I'm saying this conditionally but I'm certain as far as the document that I showed is concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we leave it to that, unless you revisit the matter. We'll consider that handwriting such as signatures, et cetera, is considered to be part of the document and to be considered by the Chamber. Then you tendered them. No objections. Mr. Registrar, 65 ter 28623, the chart itself, receives number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P683, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is admitted into evidence. 65 ter 09996 receives number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P684, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. 65 ter 10071.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P685, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted. Next one, 65 ter 10072.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P686, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted. Next one, 10235.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P687, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted. 65 ter 10646.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P679, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. 6 --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: For clarification of the record, Your Honour, 689. And Exhibit -- 65 ter 1023 --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: -- 5 receives Exhibit 686, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, 687, I take it. Let's re-start at 10072. That one received P686. The next one, 10235, receives number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Next one is 65 ter 10646.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P688, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted. 65 ter 10647.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P689, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted. 65 ter 13713.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P690, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. 65 ter 13726.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P691, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted. 65 ter 27078.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P692, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. Ms. D'Ascoli.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, to finish I would tender the stage of associated exhibits listed in the exhibit list for Mr. Mandilovic. I can read the 65 ter numbers individually, if that assists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, before we start reading numbers, but perhaps we take them one by one. It is it quite a -- associated exhibits --

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: I think we should start from number 10246.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's a huge number, Ms. D'Ascoli.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: We're aware of that, Your Honours, but it is for the same purposes. We reduced already almost half the list of associated exhibits associated to the witness statement. The remaining one which I believe are 24 are all medical records, all related to victims of Scheduled Incidents and again the purpose of tendering them at this stage is for having the benefit of this witness authentifying the documents as he did in the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So primary purpose is authentication of these documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. If it only has to do with the medical part of this document, as was the case previously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I suggest that you provide the Registrar with a list with the twenty-four 65 ter numbers, that the representative of the Registry provides provisionally P numbers and the Chamber will then decide on admission. And since there's no objection, there's a fair chance that we would.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: We will do that, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we will proceed in that fashion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mandilovic, this concludes your testimony in this courtroom. I'd like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and for having answered all the questions, questions put to you by the parties, questions put to you by the Bench, and I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the next witness, unless there's any reason not to proceed --

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, the next witness is ready [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... after the break. But before we take a break, I'd like to deliver a decision in relation to protective measures. The Chamber will now deliver its decision on the Prosecution motion for protective measures for Witness RM045. On the 25th of October, 2012, the Prosecution requested protective measures of pseudonym and face distortion for Witness RM045. The Defence did not respond to this request. The Chamber has set out in a previous decision the test it applies when considering whether to grant protective measures. In this respect, the Chamber refers the parties to its 15th of August, 2012, decision on Prosecution motion for protective measures for Witness RM115. Witness RM045 is a Muslim and his family resides in a predominantly Bosnian Serb area in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The witness's testimony is expected to relate to events that occurred in that same area and may antagonise other persons living in that area. Based on the description of the witness's family situation in the motion, the Chamber is satisfied that there is ethnic tension in the area concerned. The Chamber also takes into consideration that the Defence did not oppose this submission. Further, the Chamber considers that the right of the accused to a public trial is only marginally affected by granting the requested protective measures. Under the circumstances noted above, and given that the Defence did not object to the request, the Chamber decides to grant the protective measures of pseudonym and face distortion for Witness RM045. And this concludes the Chamber's decision. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I suggest that we take a few minutes to deal with another matter as well as Mr. Traldi has a preliminary matter with respect to the next witness. Perhaps it might be a useful way of using this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If it's just takes a few minutes, then we could proceed before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, on Friday during the re-direct examination of Witness van der Weijden, Exhibit P677 was marked for identification pending the Prosecution providing the Chamber with some information about the provenance of the document. The Prosecution can now provide that additional information. The document was listed as GS VRS Annex number 7, programme for a sniper course in the VRS, dated 1995. This document is part of the Drina Corps collection which was provided to the Office of the Prosecutor by authorities of the RS Ministry of Interior in Banja Luka field office on the 13th of December, 2004. With that, Your Honour, the Prosecution would renew its tendering of that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, in view of the information provided is there any objection or --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could you please hear Mr. Ivetic on this, because it's his witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, off the top of my head I believe that was the only objection that we had respect to that document. I think it was actually a matter raised by the Chamber. I don't I think I actually formulated it as an objection, per se, but I would think that's -- the provenance of the document has been cleared up and it was used in the re-direct than it ought to -- ought to come into evidence [Overlapping speakers] ... objection made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, P677 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, we'll be guided whether you wish to hear Mr. Traldi address you on some matters related to the next witness now or before when we return from the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It also depends on how much time it would take. If it is short we have an opportunity to consider it during the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I think it's about five minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Traldi, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You Honour, there are two preliminary matters I would like to address, in one public and one in private. First, in its reply to our 92 ter motion for Witness RM79, the Defence objected to the addition of two documents to our Rule 65 ter exhibit list. The Defence agreed in December that we could address that issue orally at this point. That's on the record at transcript page 6154. For your reference the documents have been uploaded into e-court as 65 ter 28613 and 28614. At this point, I would just quickly note for the record that the documents were disclosed on 30 November in batch 49 prior to the filing of the response. Otherwise, I propose to deal with this matter when it arises during the examination if the Defence maintain their objections, if that's agreeable to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's agreeable to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And for the other issue, I would request that we go into private session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. We'll take a break, and we'll resume at 20 minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there are no preliminaries, the witness can be escorted into the courtroom. Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honour, while the witness is being brought in, I just put on the record that I have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You can proceed bringing in the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: That I have reviewed the Chamber's decisions on the adjudicated facts, and I will be restricting my examination, to some extent, on the basis of facts 1234, through 1240, including not tendering 65 ter 5998 during examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mrs. Selmanovic. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I invite you to stand and make the solemn declaration -- if you -- if you have difficulties in standing, there's no problem. Is it ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated, Mrs. Selmanovic. Mrs. Selmanovic, you will first be examined by Mr. Traldi. Mr. Traldi is counsel for the Prosecution. And you will find him to your right. Please proceed, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Good afternoon, ma'am. Could you please state your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Munira Selmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, ma'am, do you recall giving a statement to this Tribunal in 2009?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd ask the Court Officer to call 65 ter 27970 to our screens and zoom in on the signature on the bomb left side of the first page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What's the number, Mr. Traldi?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: If we could zoom in to the bottom left-hand side of the first page, next to the word "signature" in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Ma'am, is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'd ask that the Court Officer call up page 9 and zoom in on the signature, this time near the top of the page. Is that also your signature, ma'am?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the zooming in --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- if that's large enough for the witness to look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, ma'am, is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Was your statement read to you in preparation for your testimony here?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: In preparation, you made three very specific corrections to your statement, and I'm just going to remind you of those now. In paragraph 6 of your statement, page 3 of the English and B/C/S you mention that Rade Dubovina visited Novoseoci shortly before the massacre on 22 September 1992 with his sister. Is it right that you are not sure which of his sisters was with him?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sure about Momirka -- I mean, I think it was Momirka.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: In paragraph 13, page 5 of the English and pages 4 and 5 of the B/C/S, you mention some soldiers who were at Metaljka field on 22 September 1992. Was there also a soldier named Milenko Koprivica there at that time?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And in paragraph 20 of your statement, page 6 of the English and B/C/S, you say Momcilo Pajic boarded your bus from Novoseoci to Sarajevo that day before it left to make sure none of the men from Novoseoci had gotten on. Was that Momcilo Pajic or Milorad Savic who boarded the bus?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. It was Milorad Savic, not Momcilo Pajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Subject to those corrections, ma'am, if I were to ask you the same questions you were asked when your statement was taken, would you give the same answers, in substance?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And now that you have sworn to testify truthfully, do you affirm the truthfulness and accuracy of this statement?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: I confirm that it is true. There's nothing in it but the truth, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender 65 ter 27970, pursuant to Rule 92 ter as a public exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The usual sequence is to ask the witness whether the witness would give the same answers. Or is that -- I'm just, yep, I see that it's there. Yes. No objections, Mr. Stojanovic. Mr. Registrar, the number would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P717, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P717 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will now very briefly summarise the witness's written evidence for the public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have explained to the witness the purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I have, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Munira Selmanovic is from Sokolac municipality. On 22 September 1992 she and the other Muslims from her village of Novoseoci were summoned to Metaljka field. When she went home to take out her disabled father she found that their house had been looted and her father was covered in blood. Serb soldiers separated the men, including, Mrs. Selmanovic's husband and teenage son, from the women and children and some elderly people. The women, children, and elderly were taken to buses and after a soldier inspected the buses to make sure no men had boarded, they were driven towards Sarajevo. Mrs. Selmanovic never saw her husband or the other men detained at Metaljka again. Your Honours, that completes the summary, and I will have some questions now for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may put them to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Ma'am, I want to start off with some information about your village of Novoseoci. Were there Serb villages nearby?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were. There were a number of Serb villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And before the war, what were your relationships like with the people in those Serb villages?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: We were on good terms, very good terms. No one had any negative feelings towards others. We went along and agreed finally.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd ask that 65 ter 06863 be called to our screens. It is a report dated 28 July 1992, which identifies itself as being from a SRK command.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Ma'am, I'm going to move now to the summer of 1992 and I'm going read a little bit of the document for you. The document, for your reference, is dated 28 July 1992, and it says about villages including, Novoseoci - this is at top of the page 2 in the English - that the villages are "peaceful for now. They are not causing problems for the Serbian population ..." And I'm going to ask you three very specific questions about this document. First, was there any armed conflict in Novoseoci in the summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: No. There was no armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And did your village have any problems with the neighbouring Serb villages at that time?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: No, it did not. Never any.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Finally, the report claims that there were extremists in Novoseoci at the time. Were you aware of any extremists in Novoseoci?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: No, we were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd ask that 65 ter 06863 be admitted into evidence as the next public Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P718, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P718 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And I'd ask that 65 ter 8292 be called to our screens. It's a document dated 26 September 1992, which identifies itself as coming from the 2nd Romanija Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, ma'am, I'm going to turn now to the events of 22 September 1992. Mrs. Selmanovic, this document describes furniture being taken from a home in Novoseoci by a soldier. On 22 September 1992, did you see soldiers taking goods out of your own home?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And this document also refers to a soldier in the VRS "moving into a house in Novoseoci" which he had chosen to live in. Did you come to learn whether anyone used your house right after you left in September 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't find out whether someone used it. The house was in good order. Once things were over, we learned that some soldiers were billeted there. I didn't learn of anyone actually living there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, so, is it correct that those are Serb soldiers who were billeted there during the war?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender 65 ter 8292 into evidence as the next public Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P719, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P719 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Ma'am, you mention in paragraph 10 of your statement, now Exhibit P717 on page 4 of the English and B/C/S, that you saw armed soldiers when you arrived at Metaljka field on 22 September 1992. Can you tell the Judges what those soldiers looked like.

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: The soldiers were all in uniforms. Some were olive-drab, others camouflage. Some were armed while others had some kind of short rifles and hand-grenades around their belt. So this is what is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I want to talk now, ma'am, about your husband. You say in paragraph 23 of P717, at page 7 of the English and B/C/S, that your husband was at Metaljka and his body wasn't found where the other people who were there were found. Have his remains ever been found?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was with our other men. However, his body was only found last year. His body was moved to another mass grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I'd ask that the Court Officer please call up 65 ter 28613. It is a document dated 27 September 1999 coming from Sokolac municipality. And, just for reference, this is one of the two documents to which the Defence had objected.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Ma'am, do you remember providing a copy of your husband's death certificate to the Office of the Prosecutor this past November?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And is this that death certificate, ma'am?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I'd inquire first whether the Defence maintains their objection to adding this document. But if they do not, then I'd tendered it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we maintain our objection, which we submitted as part of our written submission of the 16th of December, 2012, and the arguments we put forth regarding its disclosure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Also in view of the fact that it was provided to the Prosecution rather recently? I mean, ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. It was disclosed to us on the 30th of November, as my esteemed colleague said. On the 4th of December, we filed our response objecting, because even up to that point in time, we were objectively unable to open the file to see which two documents it contained. It also resulted in our being in the position to object to this kind of disclosure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you -- could you -- I do understand that the document was provided by the witness to the Prosecution only this year, if I'm --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: On 16 November, 2012.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 16th of November. Now, could you tell us what the prejudice is you have, Mr. Stojanovic. I think you asked for another 90 days to study this one-page document. Is that ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it concerns two documents that were provided at the same time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no. At this time we're dealing with the first one, 28613. Could you explain to this Chamber what is the problem in six weeks to look at this document and to -- what would you need more at this moment? To what extent is it prejudicial if it would be added to the 65 ter list and admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We don't know whether it would be detrimental or not, or prejudicial. However, it was our intention to do a background check to see how it was issued, on what grounds, and to also check the location where the body was found in the secondary grave. All that is necessary to corroborate the accuracy and truthfulness of this document. It is the only reason that we stated on the 14th of December.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Isn't it true that this document dates from 1999 when the body was not yet retrieved, not yet found. So, therefore, what could the comparison -- what could it reveal, which is relevant for the admission of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely, Your Honour. The document was issued in 1999; that is to say, before the body was found as was confirmed by the witness today. In other words, this document should be accompanied by an administrative decision that the person was proclaimed dead, and we all -- we need all of that to see how the whole procedure developed and what was the basis for the issuance of this document. When the document was issued, according to our knowledge, the body had still not been found.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber allows adding the document to the 65 ter list. And I take it that you want to tender it as well --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Mr. Traldi. And, Mr. Registrar, the number to be assigned would be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter number 28613 shall be assigned Exhibit P720.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P720 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Stojanovic, if you want to further explore or investigate the background of this document, you may revisit the matter once you have results of those investigations.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Ma'am, in paragraph 21 of P717, at page 7 of the English and B/C/S, you provide the names of certain people you last saw on 22 September 1992. In preparation for your testimony here, did you prepare a list of names as well which you provided to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd ask that 65 ter 28614 be called to our screens. For reference, this is the other document to which the Defence objection applied.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Ma'am, is this the list you provided to us?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And in the bottom right-hand corner of the B/C/S version, is that your signature and the date you provided us with the list?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Do you remember seeing all of the people on this list at Metaljka on 22 September 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: The first 14 people on the list all have the same last name, Selmanovic. Were they all members of your husband's family?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: They were all members of his family, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Amir Selmanovic, at number 12, his name is underlined. Why -- why is it underlined?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: It is underlined because, out of the entire group, his body was the only one that has never been found. Everyone else was found, save for Amir, and that is the truth of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: In your statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I interrupt.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is Amir Selmanovic, number 12, somebody other than Amir Selmanovic at number 2?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: They're one and the same person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. This is Memic's son and the other person is Mustafa Selmanovic's son.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And just for clarity, ma'am, is it Amir, son of Memic, or Amir, son of Mustafa, whose body has not yet been found?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: Memic's son Amir. That's the one.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: At number 45 on the list, we see Devla Karic. You say in paragraph 14 of P717 that she had been sent to get her husband from Metaljka. Who sent her to get her husband?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: The army sent her. And Milorad Savic -- no, sorry, Momcilo Pajic. They said we all had to assemble. Momcilo Pajic sent her to fetch her husband.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And other than Devla, were the people on this list all still alive when you were taken to the buses that took you to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: They were all alive, once we were put on the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Did you ever see any of them alive again?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: No, never. Not one.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, ma'am, I have three specific questions about the list itself before we move on. First, who wrote down the names on the list?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: I signed the list, and the list was comprised by my cousin.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We didn't hear the name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't know all of the persons on the list by name, and she helped me out to fill everyone in. All of them were our friends or in-laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Ma'am, was that person named Muniba Colic?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: Muniba Colic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Regarding names that she helped you remember, for Sejo Pavic, Hasib Colic, Adem Catic, and Ismet Hadzic, did you remember their names yourself or did Muniba help remind you?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: I did not understand.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... could.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] didn't understand, Sejo what?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continued] The booth did not get the names. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you repeat the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps take them one by one.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: For Sejo Pasic did you remember that name yourself or did Muniba help remind you?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: Sejo Pasic, Ceko's in-law. We recalled him. He was one of ours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And is it right then to say that she helped you remember the name during the process of putting the list together?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Did you remember seeing that person at Metaljka and forget his name, or did you not remember seeing him?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: I remember his name, and I remember that he stayed at Metaljka, together with the others listed here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I'm conscious of the time. There are three more names in this exhibit and for continuity, I would suggest that if it is amenable to everyone we deal with it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you may put the next three names to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: For Hasib Colic, is that a name that you remember yourself before you wrote the list, or is it a name that you and Muniba remembered when you were putting the list together?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: I remember Nezim Colic. Hasib Colic was his relative and I recall them, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, ma'am, I'd ask you to focus on a very specific question. When you were writing the list, was it you or Muniba who remembered his name?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: I remember the names too. But I couldn't necessarily put a first and last name together and she could remember her family better. She was at her father's and could remember her husband's family members as well, and she recalls the whole situation and the whole group better than I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Then Adem Catic. Is that a name that she helped you remember or one that you remembered independently?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: She helped me out there. All of those who belonged to her family, they are the ones she helped me with.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And Ismet Hadzic. Is that another one that she helped you out with?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: Ismet Hodzic [as interpreted]. We had known him from before, and she did help me out but I did know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And for the other 41 people had you remembered the names yourself?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I recalled all of them. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And for those four, did you remember seeing them at Metaljka and forget their names, or did you not remember seeing them?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: Every person on the list was there at that moment. But I couldn't exactly recall this or that person, and to help myself out, I made a list. I remembered the Selmanovics and Karics who lived in our village. As for the rest, they were friends and in-laws, and I needed some help there. But I remember them all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, with that I tender 65 ter 28614, noting that it's one of the other exhibits to which the Defence had objected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I suggest that we adjourn first and that Mr. Stojanovic thinks about his objections, whether they stand or not, and deal with them on Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I heard that you said Wednesday. I don't know if the Chamber saw our earlier e-mail, we expect to be much quicker than we originally anticipated with our direct examination tomorrow --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I haven't seen it. If that is the case I will inform the witness that it is uncertainty when we will resume.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mrs. Selmanovic, tomorrow, we will not immediately continue with your testimony. There is a chance that we would continue later during the morning or early in the afternoon, but there also is a chance that we can only resume on Wednesday. So, therefore, we'd like to you remain stand-by in the second half of tomorrow morning's morning session, and you will be informed about whether it will be tomorrow or on Wednesday when you resume your testimony. Mr. Traldi, how much time would you still need?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honour, we estimated 45 minutes, which I believe leaves me another 15. I will be several minutes shorter than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mrs. Selmanovic, I want to instruct you that you should not speak with anyone about your testimony, whether that is the testimony you have given today or whether that is testimony still to be given tomorrow or the day after tomorrow. Not to speak or communicate in any other way with whomever about your testimony. Is that clear to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then you may follow the usher. We do know yet whether we will see you again tomorrow or on Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by your leave, about the schedule, we had announced two and a half hours for this witness, having in mind the witness's status, we believe that we will need less time and I believe we can fit in the schedule in that way. I believe we will need under two hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that information. We adjourn for the day, and we'll resume tomorrow, Tuesday, the 15th of January, at 7.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, III.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 15th day of January, 2013, at 7.30 a.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
